Maladaptive Strategies.value: push away positive emotions because they feel unsafe
try hard not think about the trauma
Watching TV programmes/ films or reading about similar events

Threat.value: Taking too many risks or doing things that could cause you harm
I am on high alert when I hear unexpected or loud sounds

Memory.value: Sometimes I feel the full emotional intensity of the event without any clear image or memory
The memory feels like it belongs to someone else rather than to me
I cannot put the memories of the event in the right order

There is something wrong with me as a person

issues.item: Threat: Intrusion Monitoring: I listen for sounds that might mean someone is entering my home
issues.explanation: These items imply a trauma involving a direct interpersonal assault by a perpetrator with ongoing home-intrusion danger. That is hard to reconcile with the validated trauma type of witnessed other trauma, where the patient observed trauma happening to someone else rather than being personally harmed.

issues.item: Maladaptive Strategies: Avoid Perpetrator Cues: Anything that reminds me of the person who harmed me
issues.explanation: The rest of the profile is broadly coherent for PTSD with strong links among triggers, threat, appraisals, and memory, but these two items specifically shift the narrative to a victim-of-assault formulation rather than a witness formulation.

vignette:
At 77, Minh Tran still carried himself with the careful posture of a surgeon, though in recent months he had begun to feel less steady in the operating room and more easily thrown by small disturbances around him. Born in South East Asia and now long settled in the United States with his wife, he remained proud of the life he had built through medicine. Yet the event he had witnessed years earlier had come to sit uncomfortably beneath that identity. During a long shift, he had been present when another person was badly burned. The details that stayed with him were not arranged neatly in his mind. He could not always place the sequence in order, and when he tried to recall it, the memory felt oddly remote, as if it belonged to someone else rather than to him. At times he had no clear picture at all, only a sudden rush of the same emotional force he had felt then, the same dread and helpless intensity, arriving without an image to anchor it.

Certain sensations could bring that state on immediately. A hot patch on his skin, a temperature that felt too close to the conditions of the original event, could make him recoil before he had time to think. The smell of something burnt was especially potent. It could appear in the kitchen, in a hallway, in a parking lot where someone had left a cigarette smoldering, and for a moment he would be back in the atmosphere of danger, alert in a way that felt physical rather than remembered. He also noticed that stress in general made him vulnerable; on days when the demands of the hospital, family responsibilities, or the ordinary pressures of aging accumulated, he felt his body bracing itself as though another crisis were about to break open. He had come to believe that his body kept reacting as if he were still in danger even when he was safe, and that conviction had become hard to shake.

In the months after the event, Minh found himself trying to shut it away. He worked hard not to think about it and learned to steer his mind elsewhere whenever the memory began to rise. He avoided television programmes and films that showed similar injuries, and he skipped articles or news reports that might contain the same kind of scene. Positive moments became difficult in their own way. When his wife tried to draw him into pleasure or celebration, he sometimes pushed those feelings away because they seemed unsafe, as if relaxation would make him careless and leave him exposed to another shock. He did not describe this to others in dramatic terms; instead, he simply became more reserved, less willing to linger in joy, as though keeping emotion at a distance might keep him intact.

The sense of threat remained close to the surface. Minh was jumpy and easily startled, especially by unexpected or loud sounds. In the hospital, a dropped metal tray, an abrupt alarm, or a raised voice in the corridor would make him tense before he could identify what had happened. At home, a sharp noise from the television or a pan hitting the stove could set his heart racing. Even outside the clinic he stayed on alert when he heard sudden sounds, scanning automatically for what might be wrong. That vigilance had become part of how he moved through the day, and he spoke of needing to be especially careful because you never know what can happen next. Alongside that caution, there were moments when he took too many risks or did things that could cause him harm, as if ordinary concern for his own safety had become less convincing to him than the urge to push forward and ignore the warning signs.

These experiences left him unsettled about himself. Minh could be exacting and outwardly composed, but privately he had started to wonder whether there was something wrong with him as a person. He was troubled that, despite his profession and years of training, his own body seemed unwilling to stand down. He worried about what it meant that a smell, a sound, or a temperature on his skin could pull him into such distress. The contrast between who he had been and how he now felt was painful to him, and it made him question his own reliability.

What brought him to seek help was the accumulation of these moments: the startle that embarrassed him in public, the constant readiness that exhausted him, and the sense that he could no longer simply reason his way out of the reactions. He had begun to worry that he was living too narrowly, avoiding reminders, holding back from pleasure, and carrying himself as if danger were always nearby. At this stage, he wanted relief from the bodily alarm that kept returning and from the private fear that something in him had become permanently altered.
